advisor_letter:
Dear [[CLIENT_NAME]],

You are standing at an important threshold. With retirement about three years away, the next few years carry more weight than the thirty that follow, and it is natural to wonder whether what you have built will be enough to live the way you want. This letter, and the report behind it, is here to look at that question calmly and with real numbers rather than guesswork.

You have done meaningful work to get here. You have set aside savings across a few different accounts, and your retirement income would rest mostly on the public benefits you have earned over a lifetime of contributing. That foundation is steady, and your personal savings sit on top of it as a helpful complement. These are the building blocks the rest of this report examines.

Here is what each part of the report would give you. The executive summary delivers the verdict in about thirty seconds. Chapter I lays out the foundations and the projection of how your money could behave over time. Chapter II describes the risks you would be taking on. Chapter III walks through strategies and the decisions in front of you. Chapter IV offers alternatives you might test. I encourage particular attention to Chapter II, where the report is honest about what could put pressure on the plan.

My hope is that you finish this report feeling clearer and more in control, not more anxious. The numbers tell a reassuring story overall, with a few areas worth watching. Please remember that this is AI-assisted analysis of your projection, not personal advice. Consult a certified financial planner before acting on any observation in this report.

Warm regards,
Your BuildFi analyst
overall_assessment: Your plan reaches a success rate of **91%**, which is very solid. Its greatest strength is a dependable public-income floor from CPP/OAS, with GIS likely adding support at your income level, so the bulk of your monthly needs would be covered no matter how markets behave. The main risk appears to be spending: if costs rose meaningfully, the picture would tighten quickly, and keeping spending close to today's level would protect the plan the most. Consult a certified financial planner.
verdict: In the typical scenario, savings could finish near **20K$**, while a cautious scenario lands around **7K$** and a favourable one near **35K$**. The spread stays narrow because your income leans on steady public benefits rather than the ups and downs of markets, which keeps the range predictable.
page_zero_verdict: Heading into retirement on your own, you seem most concerned with knowing your everyday costs would be covered for the rest of your life. That is exactly what this report sets out to look at.
profile_summary: You hold about **54K$** in savings, split across an RRSP (18K$), a TFSA (32K$), and a small non-registered account (4K$). Your money is balanced fairly evenly between growth and safer holdings, which suits someone whose income rests mainly on guaranteed public benefits.
trajectory_insight: Across 5000 simulated futures, savings would typically settle near **20K$**, with a cautious scenario near **7K$** and a favourable one near **35K$**. The range stays narrow because your dependable public income carries most of the load, and the typical path does not run out.
income_insight: Your guaranteed income coverage reaches **98%**, meaning public benefits would cover almost all of your monthly needs, leaving only a small gap of about **$50** a month. OAS is the dominant source, supported by CPP, so your everyday costs would rest on a steady foundation.
taxInsight: Your taxes in retirement would be very light, with a lifetime tax of just **855$** and an effective rate near 1.3% against your income. There would be no years where OAS is reduced by clawback, so none of your benefit would be lost to higher-income rules. The main lever here is simply the order in which you draw from your accounts, since pulling from your TFSA stays tax-free and keeps reported income low. Living in Ontario, your lower income keeps you well within the gentlest tax brackets, so further tax savings are modest. Consult a certified financial planner.
estateInsight: Your projected net estate would be about **35K$**, and because your savings are modest and largely tax-sheltered, there would be no tax at death (0$) beyond a small probate cost. In a cautious scenario the estate could be closer to 13K$.
gis_insight: At your income level you would likely qualify for GIS in 24 years of retirement, adding meaningful support to your public-income floor. GIS is income-tested and reduces by roughly 50 cents for every extra dollar of certain income, so drawing from your TFSA, which does not count, would help keep that support intact.
riskInsight: The gap between a cautious outcome (**7K$**) and a favourable one (**35K$**) is narrow, reflecting how steady your income is, though savings could be depleted near age 82 in tougher conditions. Of the factors tested, a change in investment returns moves the result the most, while inflation has a smaller effect.
stress_interpretation: The plan holds up well under most pressures, staying near 91% under stagflation and even rising to 93% with persistent inflation. Its one clear weak spot is higher spending: a sharp, sustained increase in costs would drop success to just 9%, the largest swing by far. The pattern is clear: markets would not break this plan, but steady spending is what keeps it intact.
